title: Personalization without context can make the experience worse
description: Personalizing isn't automatically useful. Use relevant context, explain recommendations and let people correct what the system assumed.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: recommendations and automations that show the why and can be adjusted by the people who use them.

blocks.text: Personalizing an experience seems like an obvious choice: if the product knows the person, it can show more relevant content, anticipate needs and cut steps.
But personalization isn't automatically useful. A recommendation can feel invasive, an interface can hide important options and an automation can reinforce a wrong assumption about the user.
The challenge isn't to personalize as much as possible. It's deciding when personalization helps, which data justifies that decision and how the person stays in control of the experience.
Personalization needs to solve a problem

Before creating a personalized experience, describe the expected benefit: cutting the time it takes to find a feature, highlighting content relevant to a task, remembering a chosen preference or keeping someone from repeating information.
If there's no clear benefit, personalizing may only add complexity to the product.
Tell declared preference apart from inferred behavior
There's a difference between a person choosing weekly notifications and the system inferring they want more messages because they opened several notifications.
Declared preferences are usually easier to explain and correct. Behavioral inferences can be wrong or lose validity over time.
When a personalization depends on an important inference, give the person a way to understand, adjust or turn off that choice. Avoid presenting assumptions as facts.
Don't turn personalization into a black box
If the interface changes without explanation, the person may think they lost a feature or that the product is inconsistent.
A few practices help:

items: Explain why a recommendation shows up when that influences the decision
Let people change filters or preferences
Offer a way to correct bad recommendations
Avoid hiding essential information in the name of a “simpler” experience
Flag when content is sponsored or influenced by commercial interests.

blocks.text: Personalization should support autonomy, not reduce choices without the person noticing.
Watch out for the feedback loop

Recommendation systems can reinforce their own results. If a person gets more content of one type, they start interacting with it more because that's what is visible. The system may read that behavior as a definitive preference and narrow the variety even further.

Evaluate not just clicks and time spent, but also perceived relevance, diversity of results, ability to find alternatives and how easy it is to correct recommendations. Metrics should reflect the product's context and the risk of narrowing options.
Measure value and side effects
A personalized experience can increase clicks and still hurt satisfaction or the discovery of alternatives. Define a primary metric tied to the goal and guardrail metrics tied to possible harm.
A hypothetical example for a content platform:

items: Goal: help people find relevant content.
Primary metric: share of sessions in which the person finds and opens content they consider useful.
Guardrail metrics: topic diversity, hidden recommendations, negative feedback and how easy it is to find content outside the recommendations.

blocks.text: Don't use these metrics as a universal recipe. Adapt them to the user's job and check whether they reflect a good experience.
Give control without turning settings into a maze
Control doesn't mean exposing dozens of options on a complex screen. It means letting the person understand and change important decisions.

Start with simple controls, like “show less of this”, “don't use this preference” or “edit my interests”, when they fit the product. Explain the effect of each control and give feedback after the change.
Test whether people understand why they got a recommendation and whether they can correct the result. If the control technically exists but nobody can find it, it isn't solving the problem.
Well-designed personalization isn't the one that knows the most about the person. It's the one that uses relevant context in a way that is useful, transparent and correctable.
